title: The Communist Party of Xi Jinping
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Effect of policies and politics of other countries on India's interests · GS3 › Security challenges in border areas
summary: The CPC's fifth plenum confirmed sweeping purges, left the Central Military Commission with two members, and expelled the former chief of the command that faces India on the LAC.
ideas: Discipline over capacity: the plenum's theme was 'rigorous self-governance of the Party'; 33 members and alternates were expelled (14 a year ago), and attendance was the lowest since the Mao era.
GS2 · China's internal politics
Xi is choosing understaffed but loyal institutions over efficient but suspect ones.
A hollowed-out high command: the Central Military Commission, long a seven-member body, now has two members, Xi and discipline chief Zhang Shengmin, who was elevated to the Politburo mid-term.
GS2 · China / GS3 · Security
A two-member CMC commanding the world's largest military concentrates power and weakens checks.
Purges reach Xi's inner circle: removals include former vice-chairman Zhang Youxia, former Western Theatre commander Wang Haijiang and two directors of Xi's military secretariat.
GS2 · China
When the purge reaches the leader's own secretariat, fear rather than performance shapes careers.
Risk for India on the LAC: the Western Theatre Command, which is responsible for the LAC, has seen its former chief expelled; commanders may prove loyalty through assertiveness, not restraint.
GS3 · Border security / GS2 · India–China
Political purges in the PLA can make LAC commanders more assertive, raising the risk of incidents.
Errors stop travelling upward: when every cadre watches his back, bad news rarely reaches the top; and China's military production will likely be sustained, so turmoil is no reassurance.
GS2 · Policies of other countries
Purge-driven systems hide errors, so India should not read Chinese turmoil as weakness.
keywords: China's top military body, chaired by Xi
With the CMC reduced to two members, military command in China is more centralised than ever.
The PLA formation responsible for the LAC with India
Turmoil in the Western Theatre Command bears directly on stability along the LAC.
Proving allegiance through visible assertive action
Under purges, commanders may engage in loyalty signalling through assertive moves on the border.
Bad news failing to reach the top in a climate of fear
Purges create an information bottleneck in which errors rarely travel upward.
The next CPC congress, due in October 2027
Personnel churn ahead of the 21st Party Congress will shape China's posture towards India.
examples: Two-member CMC
A body that was long seven-member now has only Xi and his discipline chief
GS2 · China / GS4 · Concentration of power
China's two-member CMC shows how anti-corruption drives can concentrate power.
Expelled Western Theatre commander
The former chief of the command facing India was among those removed
GS3 · Border management
The expulsion of the Western Theatre commander shows why India must watch China's internal politics for border risk.
pyqs: China's trade surplus and military power, and its impact on India.
Security challenges along the China border: an assertive LAC command is one.
China's BRI and great-power competition in South Asia.
China as a challenge greater than the Soviet Union for the US.

trend.t: China questions moved from economic and military power and its impact on India (2017) and CPEC (2014, 2018) to China in global power competition (2021) and the BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of rivalry (2026). GS3 tested border security with China and Pakistan (2024).
trend.watch: China is asked almost every few years across GS2 and GS3, usually through India's security and neighbourhood. Prepare China's internal drivers along with the LAC and the BRI.
focus: China in South Asia: BRI and CPEC
Decoding China's internal politics for India

potential: How do internal political developments in China affect India's security interests along the Line of Actual Control? Discuss. (10 marks)
"Centralisation of power in China's military leadership may make the India–China border less, not more, predictable." Examine. (15 marks)

practice.q: How do internal political developments in China affect India's security interests along the Line of Actual Control? Discuss.
parts: How China's internal politics affects the LAC

answer.t: The CPC's fifth plenum confirmed 33 expulsions and left the CMC with two members, while the former chief of the Western Theatre Command, which faces India, was expelled.

pts.t: Officers may prove loyalty through assertiveness, not restraint.
A two-member CMC means fewer checks on risky moves.
Errors and local incidents may not be reported upward in time.
Pressure at home can turn into firmness abroad.
Military production is likely to continue despite purges.
Churn complicates military talks and confidence-building.
Border infrastructure, surveillance and force posture.
Corps-commander talks and hotlines.
Deeper expertise to read Chinese politics.
Quad and coordination with like-minded states.

answer.t: India must read purges in Beijing as a source of risk, not relief, and pair firm deterrence with open channels on the LAC.

title: Tactical calculations should not overlook dangers of terror: EAM
where: Politics, page 7 (Shubhajit Roy); The World page for the G20 photo row and the Canada–EU summit
syllabus: GS2 › Bilateral, regional and global groupings; Important international institutions · GS3 › Terrorism; Security of sea lanes
summary: At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar warned against tolerating terrorism for tactical gain and spoke for seafarers, freedom of navigation and fair access to markets.
ideas: Terror is not a tool: Jaishankar said tactical calculations should not hide the dangers of terrorism, which has hurt even its practitioners; a veiled reference to US engagement with Pakistan.
GS2 · India's foreign policy / GS3 · Terrorism
India argues that tolerating terrorism for short-term strategic gain backfires on those who use it.
Diplomacy over force: on the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, he said military solutions will not work and diplomacy must be given a chance.
GS2 · India's global role
India positions itself as a voice for dialogue and diplomacy in today's conflicts.

The Global South pays for shipping attacks: attacks on civilian shipping and seafarers raise the cost of fuel, food and fertiliser; at least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia since February.
GS2 · Global South / GS3 · Maritime security
Attacks on sea lanes hit the Global South hardest through fuel, food and fertiliser prices.
Law of the sea: India called for freedom of navigation and an end to attacks under international law, especially UNCLOS, and has launched a joint initiative with Liberia to protect seafarers.
GS2 · International law / Maritime
India backs a rules-based maritime order under UNCLOS and acts on seafarer safety with Liberia.
Weaponised trade: he said the right to industrialise is being denied by flooding markets, weaponising supply chains and restricting market access, and urged resilient, alternative connectivity.
GS2 · Groupings / GS3 · Supply chains
India links economic security to de-risking supply chains and building alternative connectivity.
keywords: Using trade, supply chains or market access as coercion
The weaponisation of interdependence makes supply-chain diversification a security need.
Developing countries' claim to build manufacturing without coercion
India frames fair market access as the Global South's right to industrialise.
Right of ships to sail international waters without interference
Freedom of navigation under UNCLOS is central to India's maritime and trade interests.
Reducing over-dependence on single suppliers or partners
As the world de-risks, India pitches itself as a resilient alternative supply base.
Keeping multiple partners to reduce dependence on any one
Canada and the EU seeking closer ties beyond the US reflects strategic hedging.
data: Killed in West Asia since the war began in February
At least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia since February.
examples: India–Liberia seafarer initiative
A joint initiative to safeguard seafarers
GS4
GS2 · Maritime diplomacy / GS4 · Care for workers
India and Liberia's seafarer initiative shows diplomacy protecting ordinary workers at sea.
G20 'family photo' cancelled
The US scrapped the ministers' photo after Europeans objected to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
GS2 · Groupings
The scrapped G20 photo shows how the Ukraine war divides the grouping.
Canada–EU 'Alliance for the Future'
Canada and the EU discuss associate membership to cut dependence on the US
GS2 · Groupings / Effect of other countries' policies
Canada's move towards EU associate membership shows middle powers hedging against US unpredictability.
pyqs: The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges as the world moves from multilateralism to protectionism.
Maritime security and freedom of navigation.
Terrorism as a global threat and the UNSC's counter-terror bodies.
BRICS and the voice of the Global South.

trend.t: Groupings questions moved from SAARC and SCO (2016, 2021, 2023) to the Global South and BRICS as a counterweight (2026). Economic security entered through supply chains (2024) and protectionism (2025), while terrorism moved to a global, UN-level frame (2024).
trend.watch: The Global South and supply-chain security have come in each of the last three years. Prepare India's voice in groupings with concrete examples: G20, BRICS, seafarers, de-risking.
focus: India as voice of the Global South
Maritime security, UNCLOS and sea lanes

potential: "Economic security has become inseparable from national security." Discuss with reference to supply chains and sea lanes. (15 marks)
How has India used the G20 to raise the concerns of the Global South? Illustrate with recent examples. (10 marks)

practice.q: How has India used the G20 to raise the concerns of the Global South? Illustrate with recent examples.

answer.t: At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, India said the Global South is disproportionately bearing the cost of attacks on shipping and seafarers.

pts.t: Disrupted sea lanes raise costs for developing economies.
At least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia.
Freedom of navigation under UNCLOS.
Against market flooding and weaponised supply chains.
No tactical tolerance for terror.
Military solutions will not work; diplomacy must get a chance.
Work with BRICS, the African Union and like-minded states.
Alternative corridors and diversified supply chains.
Naval and coast-guard cooperation for sea lanes.

answer.t: India's G20 voice turns the Global South's everyday costs into an agenda for rules, routes and fair trade.

title: Siang dam: Why the project to counter China faces opposition in Arunachal
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood: relations; Bilateral agreements affecting India's interests; Effect of policies and politics of other countries on India's interests
summary: India's 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, meant to counter China's 60,000 MW upstream dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo, faces protests from the local Adi community.
ideas: Hydro-hegemony: China, the upstream power on the Yarlung Tsangpo (the Siang in India), approved a 60,000 MW project in December 2024. India, downstream, fears China could release water at will; India's 11,200 MW Siang project is pitched as a counter, and experts say India has a right to details of China's project.
GS2 · India–China / water as a strategic tool
Upstream control of the Brahmaputra lets China practise hydro-hegemony, making transboundary rivers a new front in India–China relations.

Domestic factors shape foreign policy: the Siang project's strategic logic runs into local resistance over ancestral land, livelihood and culture; experts say it cannot go ahead without the local community's cooperation.
GS2 · Domestic factors in foreign policy
The Siang protests show that India's external strategy depends on domestic consent: foreign policy begins at home.
keywords: Using upstream control of a river for power over downstream states
China's mega-dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo raises fears of hydro-hegemony over the Brahmaputra.
The leverage an upstream state has over water flowing downstream
As the upper riparian, China holds leverage over India's Brahmaputra flows.
Leaders must satisfy both foreign counterparts and domestic constituencies
The Siang project is a two-level game: countering China abroad while winning local consent at home.
examples: Adi community protests
Local residents in Arunachal's Siang belt oppose the dam over loss of ancestral land and livelihood
GS2 · Domestic factors in IR
Adi protests against the Siang dam show how local concerns can complicate a strategic project aimed at China.
pyqs: Domestic factors influencing foreign policy: the Siang protests are a fresh India–China example.

title: A visit to Baku, a gateway to a changing Eurasia
where: The Editorial Page, page 10 (C Raja Mohan)
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood – relations; Bilateral, regional and global groupings affecting India's interests; Effect of policies of other countries on India · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
summary: C Raja Mohan argues that Jaishankar's Baku visit resets ties with Azerbaijan and shows national interest outweighs religious or ethnic blocs, opening the Caucasus and Central Asia to India.
evolution: Turkic Council set up; it becomes the Organisation of Turkic States (OTS) in 2021.
Islamabad Declaration by Turkey, Azerbaijan and Pakistan backs Pakistan on Kashmir; 'Three Brothers' military exercise in Azerbaijan.
During Op Sindoor, Indian perceptions of a Turkey–Azerbaijan–Pakistan bloc harden; calls to boycott Turkey and Azerbaijan.
Jaishankar visits Baku; Azerbaijan hands the OTS chair to Turkey amid Ankara–Baku friction.
ideas: National interest outweighs religion and ethnicity: the 'Three Brothers' bloc is thinner than its rhetoric.
GS2 · Foreign policy principles
Azerbaijan's friction with Turkey shows that shared religion and ethnicity do not make a strategic bloc; national interest decides.
The Turkish factor: Azerbaijan's tilt to Pakistan came through Turkey, and Ankara–Baku friction (secularism, Israel) now loosens it, a chance for India and later a reset with Turkey.
GS2 · Turkey and West Asia
Azerbaijan's ties with Pakistan flowed through Turkey; as Ankara and Baku drift apart, India can engage Baku and, in time, reset ties with Ankara.
Central Asian states follow 'multi-vector' policies, like India's multi-alignment, and refuse to join blocs.
GS2 · Central Asia
Central Asia's multi-vector diplomacy, mirroring India's multi-alignment, makes it open to Indian engagement.
The Caucasus is a gateway: Azerbaijan borders Russia and Iran and looks across the Caspian to Central Asia.
GS2 · Connectivity / continental strategy
Azerbaijan, bordering Russia and Iran and facing Central Asia across the Caspian, is a gateway for India's continental diplomacy.
Don't give Islamabad a veto: India should seek neutrality from Pakistan's friends and work on shared interests.
GS2 · India–Pakistan / diplomacy
Engaging Pakistan's friends on shared interests is better than giving Islamabad a veto over India's diplomacy.
Prudence over passion: diplomacy driven by national interest, not social-media outrage, is the Kautilyan way.
GS4 · Ethics in international relations
As Kautilya taught, prudence and national interest, not public outrage, should guide foreign policy; the Baku reset is a case in point.
keywords: Engaging even 'hostile' countries to secure interests
The Baku reset shows productive diplomacy is possible even with countries public opinion dismisses as hostile.
Turkey's influence behind Azerbaijan's tilt to Pakistan
Azerbaijan's pro-Pakistan stance largely reflected its closeness to Turkey.
States act on interests, not shared religion or ethnicity
Shared faith or ethnicity does not make a strategic bloc; national interest does.
Transnational identity projects that have struggled against national interests
Like pan-Arabism and pan-Islamism, pan-Turkism falters on national interests.
Working with many powers without joining a bloc
Like India's multi-alignment, Central Asia's multi-vector diplomacy keeps options open.
The idea of political unity among Turkic peoples, promoted by Turkey
Pan-Turkism, like pan-Arabism before it, struggles against national interests.
Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan; Turkmenistan an observer
Even the OTS avoids becoming a military bloc; Kazakhstan's Tokayev rejected that idea.
The 'Three Brothers' partnership of Turkey, Azerbaijan and Pakistan is weaker than its label suggests.
Azerbaijan matters to India as a link on the INSTC.
India's outreach to inner Eurasia beyond its maritime focus
Engaging the Caucasus strengthens India's continental strategy alongside its Indo-Pacific focus.
Letting Pakistan's friendships dictate India's diplomacy
India should not give Islamabad a veto over its diplomatic choices.
What India seeks from Pakistan's friends
India accepts others' ties with Pakistan but seeks their neutrality in India–Pakistan disputes.
Freedom to choose partners issue by issue
Engaging Baku while keeping Armenia shows India's strategic autonomy.
Foreign policy based on interest and circles of states
Kautilya's mandala reminds us that alignments shift with interests, not sentiment.
examples: Islamabad Declaration (2021)
Turkey, Azerbaijan and Pakistan backed Pakistan's position on Kashmir
India–Pakistan diplomacy
The 2021 Islamabad Declaration showed Pakistan using friends to internationalise Kashmir.
Kazakhstan rejects a Turkic military bloc
President Tokayev opposed turning the OTS into a military alliance
Central Asian autonomy
Kazakhstan's refusal to militarise the OTS shows Central Asia guarding its sovereignty.
India–Canada turnaround
Ties revived over the past year and a half after a deep low
Pragmatic diplomacy
Like the India–Canada reset, the Baku opening shows diplomacy can repair ties with 'hostile' countries.
Azerbaijan–Turkey friction
Headscarf restrictions and Baku's ties with Israel divide the two
Limits of identity blocs
Baku's secularism and Israel ties have strained its bond with Turkey.
Kautilya's Arthashastra
Foreign policy guided by national interest and prudence (the mandala theory)
GS4
Ethics in IR
The Baku reset reflects Kautilyan prudence: engage on interests, not emotions.
pyqs: Directly relevant: Central Asia's multi-vector policy and Azerbaijan as a gateway across the Caspian.
Outside powers in Central Asia: Russia, China, Turkey and Iran all compete there.
Energy: India's energy interests in Azerbaijan add to its West Asian energy ties.
Iran's role: the INSTC runs through Iran, and sanctions shape India's Eurasian plans.
China's growing presence in Eurasia, like the BRI in South Asia, is part of great-power competition.
Directly usable: India puts strategic interest first in Baku, but seeks neutrality, not hostility, an ethically defensible realism.
National interest in bilateral ties: the Baku reset shows interests can converge.
Power guided by rationality: prudent diplomacy over public outrage.

trend.t: UPSC asks India's neighbourhood beyond South Asia mainly through Central Asia (2018 Ashgabat and outside powers, 2024 Central Asian Republics) and West Asia, especially energy (2017) and Iran (2018). The angle has moved from connectivity agreements to India's overall relations and strategic weight in the region.
trend.watch: Central Asia has come in 2018 and 2024, and West Asia and Iran repeatedly. India's 'extended neighbourhood' in Eurasia is a must-study area, beyond Pakistan and China.
focus: India's Central Asia policy: connectivity (INSTC, Chabahar), energy, security
Competition among Russia, China, Turkey and Iran in Eurasia
India's multi-alignment and balancing between rival partners (e.g. Armenia and Azerbaijan)
Pakistan's partnerships in the Islamic world and India's response

potential: Discuss the significance of the South Caucasus and Central Asia for India's continental strategy. What challenges does India face in the region? (15 marks)
'Shared religion and ethnicity do not automatically produce strategic blocs.' Examine in the context of India's relations with Turkey, Azerbaijan and Pakistan. (10 marks)
How can the International North-South Transport Corridor reshape India's access to Eurasia? Discuss its prospects and constraints. (10 marks)

practice.q: Discuss the significance of the South Caucasus and Central Asia for India's continental strategy. What challenges does India face in the region?
parts: Introduction: the Baku reset and India's Eurasian outreach (one line, with facts)
Significance of the region for India (multi-dimensional)
Way forward (15 marks, so a separate part)

answer.t: EAM Jaishankar's Baku visit (October 2026) reset ties with Azerbaijan, a gateway between Russia, Iran and Central Asia, after strains during Op Sindoor (2025).

pts.t: The region links India to Russia and Europe overland, bypassing Pakistan.
pts.ex: INSTC through Iran and the Caucasus; Chabahar.

pts.t: Caspian and Central Asian oil, gas and uranium can diversify India's supplies.
pts.ex: India's energy interests in Azerbaijan; uranium from Kazakhstan.

pts.t: Azerbaijan borders Russia and Iran; Central Asia borders China and Afghanistan.
Multi-vector states share India's preference for multi-alignment over blocs.
pts.ex: Kazakhstan rejected a Turkic military alliance.

pts.t: Stability here affects terrorism, drugs and extremism flowing from Afghanistan.
New ports, railways and customs reforms are reshaping inner Eurasia's markets.
Turkey, Pakistan's close ally, pulled Azerbaijan into a pro-Pakistan stance on Kashmir.
Pakistan and Afghanistan block India's shortest route.
BRI investment and trade give China an edge.
Moscow's security role limits outside players.
pts.ex: Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan are in the Russia-led CSTO.

pts.t: Ties with Armenia and Azerbaijan must be balanced.
INSTC and Chabahar face sanctions on Iran and funding delays.
Work with Pakistan's friends on shared interests; don't give Islamabad a veto.
Complete INSTC and Chabahar links; explore Caspian routes.
Long-term deals for oil, gas, uranium and critical minerals.
Deepen ties with Azerbaijan while keeping the Armenia partnership.
SCO and the India–Central Asia Summit as platforms.
Education, IT, health and cultural links build goodwill.

answer.t: By engaging the Caucasus and Central Asia on interests rather than identities, India can widen its continental reach beyond Pakistan's veto.

title: Japan pitches Rs 8–10 lakh cr investments in India
syllabus: GS2 › India and major powers (Japan) · GS3 › Investment models; Infrastructure
summary: A Japanese industry delegation led by the Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry pitched Rs 8–10 lakh crore of investment in Indian infrastructure and manufacturing; Japan was India's top FDI source in Q1 FY27.
ideas: Japan as India's top FDI source: in Q1 FY27 Japan overtook conventional sources like Singapore, Mauritius and the US.
GS2 India–Japan · GS3 FDI
Japan became India's top FDI source in Q1 FY27, overtaking Singapore, Mauritius and the US.

Trade and investment are the two economic pillars of India–Japan ties; the Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry's Rs 8–10 lakh crore pitch targets infrastructure, manufacturing, automobiles and high-speed rail.
GS2 · India and major powers
India–Japan ties rest on trade and investment, shown by Japanese industry's Rs 8–10 lakh crore pitch for infrastructure and manufacturing.
keywords: India and Japan's Special Strategic and Global Partnership now has a strong investment pillar.
Long-term investment that does not flee quickly
India seeks durable capital like Japan's to offset volatile capital outflows.
Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (JCCI)
Japan's main business body, which led the delegation
A JCCI-led delegation pitched Rs 8–10 lakh crore of investment in India.
Faster clearances, tax predictability, skilled manpower
Japanese investors seek faster clearances, tax predictability and skilled workers.
data: Investment pitched by Japanese industry over the next few years
Japanese industry has pitched Rs 8–10 lakh crore of investment in India over the next few years.
examples: Japanese investment in high-speed rail
Part of the proposed investments, alongside automobiles and manufacturing
Infrastructure partnership
Japan's role in India's high-speed rail is a flagship of the partnership.
pyqs: A contemporary India–Japan partnership: investment is now its strongest economic pillar.
Economic ties 'below potential' then; Japan as top FDI source now shows the shift.
Gap between pledges and actual FDI: Japan's Rs 8–10 lakh crore pitch must translate into projects.
